summary: Head I is a small oil and tempera painting on hardboard by Francis Bacon, completed in 1948 as the first of a six-head series painted for his November 1949 Hanover Gallery exhibition. Like the series, it shows a screaming figure alone in a room, focusing on the open mouth, with the upper head dissolved into formless flesh. It is the first Bacon painting to feature gold background railings or bars, a motif that later became prominent in his 1950s work, especially the papal portraits. The source of the image is unclear, though likely multiple influences such as press or war photography and Matthias Grünewald, as detected by critic Denis Farr.
one_line: Head I is a 1948 oil and tempera painting by Francis Bacon, the first of a screaming-head series shown at the Hanover Gallery in 1949.
key_facts: Head I is an oil and tempera on hardboard painting by Francis Bacon.
Francis Bacon was an Irish-born British figurative artist.
Head I is the first in a series of six heads.
The remaining heads in the series were painted the following year, 1949, in preparation for a November 1949 exhibition at the Hanover Gallery in London.
Like the others in the series, Head I shows a screaming figure alone in a room and focuses on the open mouth.
The entire upper half of the skull has disappeared, leaving only the jaw, mouth and teeth and one ear intact.
Head I is the first of Bacon's paintings to feature gold background railings or bars.
The gold railings became a prominent feature of Bacon's 1950s work, especially in the papal portraits, where they often appear as enclosing cages around the figures.
It is not known what influences were behind the image of Head I.
The influences were most likely multiple, including press or war photography.
Critic Denis Farr detects the influence of Matthias Grünewald in Head I.
